No dev team. No co-founder. Just me and Claude.
I shipped 5 products in 4 months. Here's how. 👇

I've been using one communication framework with AI — and it changed everything.

01  Manifest the goal, not the steps
Declare the long-term vision before diving into tasks. AI needs to know WHERE you're going, not just what to do next.

02  High-level first, then details
Find a workable direction first. THEN refine. Don't over-specify upfront. Let the shape emerge.

03  Always give the WHY
Not "do X" — but "do X because Y." Reasons behind requests unlock dramatically better outputs.

04  Treat AI as a smart partner
I reverse prompt. I ask it to push back. I trust its intelligence.

05  It's just good communication
Same principles that make you better with humans. Trust the intelligence. Give context. Nobody reads minds — not humans, not AI.

This isn't theory. Here's what I built with this approach:
🐾 PawPaw Story — AI bedtime stories in your family's voice (App Store)
✈️ Jobpilot — AI-powered job hunting assistant
🧭 OneCo — Builder archetype quiz

All solo. All shipped.

What's your #1 rule when working with AI?

Should I kill my products and call them skills?
I sat with that for a week. Here's where I landed. 👇

When AI dropped, I was first in line.
Tried every platform. Built whatever was on my mind.
A lot of those builds started with UI — just making things exist.

So I asked my agent to audit every product I've made. Sat with the metrics and the logic for a while.

And I realized: before I build anything new, I now measure three things:

01  Brand value — does this build my name in a space?

02  Emotional value — does this give someone a feeling they couldn't get elsewhere?

03  Pure functionality — does this solve a problem and get out of the way?

Here's what surprised me most:

The same product can live as two completely different things.
A skill version — just the logic, no UI.
A real product — with design decisions that make it human.

Which one to ship is the builder's call.
And that decision is the design skill.

Not every idea needs a beautiful interface.
But you should know why you're adding one — or leaving it out.

Should you kill your product and call it a skill?
